Crypto Idea

The AI Illusion

One of the most interesting things in the AI industry today, and something that remains outside the attention of 99.9% of people, is the real impact of artificial intelligence on the economy.

Hyperscalers are investing hundreds of billions of dollars in AI infrastructure. Corporations are spending billions on tokens and on attempts to integrate AI into their operations. And the entire market is being accelerated by everyone buying from each other in a loop, valuations rising, more capital flowing in, and the market continuing to expand.

But the question that I think is actually worth asking is this: how much is artificial intelligence really affecting the economy and GDP today?

I think you may be surprised, but if you try to estimate it and look at the actual data rather than the perception created by society and social media, the impact of AI on GDP today is approximately zero percent.

In simple terms, the hundreds of billions of dollars invested so far have not yet produced any noticeable additional economic growth.

Does this mean AI is useless? Of course not.

Over the next several years, there is a very high probability that this number will change and AI will genuinely create enormous additional value.

But the data we see today tells us something different. The speed at which artificial intelligence is being integrated into society, the economy, and the world has been significantly overestimated.

And at some point, these expectations will be corrected, and the entire industry will correct along with them.

📌 Cross-Chain Messaging: Why Moving Data Can Be Riskier Than Moving Tokens

Main Points
⏺ Cross-chain isn’t only token bridges — it’s also messages passed between networks
⏺ A flawed message verification model can be more dangerous than a simple wrapped-token bug
⏺ This post explains cross-chain messaging — and where security usually fails

1️⃣ Core Idea — Chain A sends Chain B a claim about an event/state, triggering logic on the destination chain.
2️⃣ Verification — the key question is who proves the message is real (light clients, validators, relayers).
3️⃣ Risk Hotspots — verification bugs, wrong assumptions, compromised multisigs/relayers.
4️⃣ Why It’s Critical — messages can mint, withdraw, or change permissions — they mutate system state.
5️⃣ How To Think — stronger proofs reduce trust, but implementation complexity (and bug surface) increases.

Final Thoughts

Tokens can be wrapped, but messages can rewrite outcomes. Cross-chain messaging is where small verification mistakes become big disasters.

➡️ South Korea confirms 22% crypto tax will cover private wallets, foreign exchanges 

🌐 South Korea has confirmed that taxable crypto income earned through overseas exchanges and private wallets will fall under its planned 22% digital asset tax when the regime takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027. Digital Asset reported on Aug. 20, citing government responses submitted to People Power Party lawmaker Kim Sang-hoon, that the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the National Tax Service said the location or custody method of a digital asset would not determine whether income from its transfer or lending is taxable. 

⭐️ Under the current framework, income from digital assets will be classified as other income, with an annual basic deduction of 2.5 million won. Income exceeding that threshold will face a 20% national tax, rising to a maximum combined rate of 22% after local income tax. The government also maintained that the tax should take effect on schedule next year, even as the People Power Party continues to call for its abolition or another delay.

⚡️ The National Tax Service said income earned by South Korean residents through the transfer or lending of digital assets would remain taxable regardless of whether the assets were held on an overseas exchange or in a private wallet. The Finance Ministry gave a similar response, saying the tax treatment does not depend on whether the income originated domestically or overseas. Transactions made through private wallets will also be treated under the same principle.

Behind the official statements and diplomatic language, two issues stand out as particularly consequential: the Russia-China gas deal and the war in Ukraine.

According to information available to us, negotiations over the “Power of Siberia 2” pipeline project are now virtually complete. The massive pipeline is designed to deliver Russian gas to China via Mongolia.

For Moscow, its completion carries major economic and strategic significance.

China has become its main energy and trading partner. Finalizing the “Power of Siberia 2” agreement would cement that shift and place Beijing at the heart of Russia’s energy strategy for decades to come.
For China, the benefits are equally clear.

The project would strengthen the security of its gas supplies while further diversifying its energy sources.

But Beijing is negotiating from a position of strength, particularly when it comes to the economic terms and the price of future gas deliveries.

It is precisely this context that gives another element of the Bishkek meeting particular significance: the war in Ukraine.

If confirmed, the claim would represent a major political signal. Since the conflict began, Beijing has repeatedly called for a political settlement and urged the resumption of negotiations.

But a specific nine-month deadline would mark a significant shift. China would no longer simply be calling for peace; it would be seeking to set a timetable for Moscow.

The timing is particularly telling. On one hand, the two leaders appear close to finalizing a strategically important energy agreement. On the other, Beijing could be asking Moscow to bring an end to a war that has placed enormous strain on European stability and international relations.

The two issues are, of course, not officially linked. But their coincidence is difficult to overlook.

Russia now depends on China for energy markets, trade and part of its economic engagement with the outside world. China, meanwhile, has acquired growing weight within the Russian economy and leverage that extends well beyond the commercial sphere.

The phrase “comprehensive strategic partnership” therefore masks a more complicated reality: the two countries remain closely aligned in their interests, but the balance of power is gradually shifting in Beijing’s favor.

“Power of Siberia 2” could become the economic symbol of this new relationship. The nine-month deadline, if confirmed, could become its political counterpart.

The message from Bishkek would then be twofold: a major Russia-China gas deal is nearing completion, while at the same time Moscow may have been given a deadline to end the war.

If this reading proves accurate, the Putin-Xi meeting could come to be seen as an important moment in the changing balance of power between the two countries — a Russia that remains formally sovereign in its strategic decisions, but whose growing economic dependence on China is giving Beijing unprecedented influence.
